topic.summary: Detailed machine-readable graph of Tor's purpose, onion routing, relay roles, circuits, onion services, history, software ecosystem, privacy use cases, threat model, attacks and limitations, and source provenance.

provenance.primary_input: User-supplied text of the Wikipedia article 'Tor (network)', redirected from 'Tor (anonymity network)'
provenance.method: Core claims are derived from the supplied article. Additional current documentation and technical explanations are explicitly marked as external references or background context.
provenance.version_freshness_warning: The supplied article contains version and network-size snapshots that can change quickly. Do not treat version numbers, relay counts, user counts, or legal/political descriptions as current unless independently checked against current official sources.
limitations: Tor is an anonymity-enhancing system, not a guarantee of absolute anonymity.
Low-latency routing cannot reliably defeat an adversary able to observe and correlate traffic at both ends.
Traffic from applications not routed through Tor Browser or a configured Tor proxy is not automatically protected.
Tor does not itself provide end-to-end encryption between an exit relay and a public Internet destination; use HTTPS or another end-to-end encrypted protocol.
Historical attack descriptions and statistics are included as claims reported by the supplied article, not as independently verified current findings.

entities.name: Tor
entities.description: A free and open-source overlay network and software ecosystem designed to make communication more difficult to trace by separating a user's network identity from destination routing through onion routing.

attributes.primary_goal: reduce linkability between source and destination
attributes.not_a_guarantee: Tor does not guarantee perfect anonymity and cannot prevent every form of traffic correlation, endpoint compromise, or user identification.
attributes.source_basis: user-supplied Wikipedia article text; see provenance and sources

entities.name: The Tor Project
entities.description: Nonprofit organization responsible for maintaining and developing Tor software and related privacy tools.

attributes.organization_type: 501(c)(3) nonprofit, as described in supplied article

entities.name: Onion routing
entities.description: A technique that wraps traffic in multiple layers of encryption and routes it through a sequence of relays, where each relay learns only the information needed for its portion of the path.

entities.name: Overlay network
entities.description: A logical network implemented on top of an underlying network, using its connectivity while providing additional routing or service behavior.

entities.name: Mix network
entities.description: A class of systems intended to make communication relationships harder to infer by relaying and transforming traffic; Tor is categorized as a mix/overlay network in the supplied article, though Tor is a low-latency design rather than a high-latency batching mixnet.

entities.name: Tor relay
entities.description: A node that forwards Tor traffic as part of a circuit. Relays are commonly operated by volunteers and have distinct roles and flags.

attributes.trust_note: A relay sees only a portion of the route and traffic metadata, depending on its role.

entities.name: Guard relay
entities.description: The entry relay selected for a client's circuits and kept relatively stable over time to reduce exposure to many potentially hostile entry nodes.

attributes.visibility: Can observe the client's network address and that the client is using Tor, but ordinarily does not know the final destination.

entities.name: Middle relay
entities.description: A relay between the guard and exit in a typical Tor circuit; forwards traffic without serving as the public Internet exit.

entities.name: Exit relay
entities.description: The relay that forwards a circuit's traffic to a destination on the public Internet for ordinary clearnet connections.

attributes.visibility: Destination commonly sees the exit relay's public IP address.
attributes.risk: Unencrypted application traffic can be observed or modified between the exit and destination; HTTPS or other end-to-end encryption is still important.

entities.name: Bridge relay
entities.description: A relay whose address is not broadly listed as a public relay, intended in part to help users connect where public Tor relays are blocked.

attributes.distribution: may be provided through bridge-distribution mechanisms or pluggable transports

entities.name: Directory authority
entities.description: A specially trusted Tor infrastructure role that votes on network status and parameters used to build the network consensus.

attributes.security_consideration: Compromise of enough authorities could undermine consensus integrity; this is a centralization/trust consideration in Tor's network design.

entities.name: Tor network consensus
entities.description: A signed, periodically updated view of network status and relay information assembled from directory-authority votes and used by clients to select relays.

attributes.update_cadence: The supplied article says authorities vote hourly; exact operational behavior may evolve.

entities.name: Tor circuit
entities.description: A temporary logical path through a sequence of Tor relays used to carry one or more TCP streams.

attributes.onion_service_path: client-side and service-side paths join through Tor rendezvous mechanisms; traffic does not exit to the public Internet

entities.name: Virtual circuit
entities.description: A logical connection established through Tor relays; Tor can multiplex TCP streams over circuits.

entities.name: Layered circuit encryption
entities.description: Tor client traffic is protected in layers so each relay removes or processes the layer intended for it, learning only the next routing step rather than the entire route.

attributes.security_property: limits any one relay's view of the complete source-to-destination relationship
attributes.caveat: Does not hide all traffic timing/volume patterns from a sufficiently positioned observer.

entities.name: Perfect forward secrecy
entities.description: A property intended to prevent later compromise of long-term keys from exposing previously recorded session traffic, when the protocol and key lifecycle provide the property.

entities.name: Transmission Control Protocol (TCP)
entities.description: Transport-layer protocol providing reliable byte-stream communication. The supplied article describes Tor as operating at the TCP stream level.

entities.name: SOCKS proxy interface
entities.description: A proxy protocol interface through which compatible applications can send traffic to a local Tor process.

attributes.port_note: Defaults can vary by configuration and deployment; verify the local configuration.

entities.name: Tor Browser
entities.description: A browser designed to route browser traffic through Tor and reduce browser-level tracking and fingerprinting.

attributes.scope: Traffic from applications outside Tor Browser is not automatically routed through Tor unless separately configured.
attributes.security_guidance: Keep it updated, use appropriate security settings, avoid identity-revealing logins when anonymity is needed, and follow official guidance.

entities.name: Onion service
entities.description: A service reachable through Tor using a cryptographic .onion address, designed to avoid revealing the service's ordinary public IP address and to support communication without leaving the Tor network.

attributes.both_sides: Can help protect the location of the service and the network location of the client.
attributes.discovery: Addresses are not globally indexed by design; a client generally needs to know the address or obtain it from a trusted source.

entities.name: Onion address (.onion)
entities.description: A special-use address used to identify a Tor onion service; modern onion addresses encode cryptographic identity material.

attributes.access_requirement: Requires Tor-capable software or a compatible route into Tor; a normal browser alone does not directly resolve .onion addresses.

entities.name: Onion-service introduction point
entities.description: A Tor relay selected by an onion service to facilitate initial contact without directly exposing the service's location to the client.

entities.name: Rendezvous point
entities.description: A Tor relay through which a client and onion service establish a connection while each side builds its own Tor path.

entities.name: Distributed hash table (DHT)
entities.description: A distributed data structure used to locate information by key across nodes. The supplied article describes onion-service information being published and discovered through distributed Tor directory mechanisms; implementation details vary by protocol version.

entities.name: Pluggable transport
entities.description: A mechanism that changes how Tor traffic appears on the network to make blocking or identification more difficult.

attributes.purpose: help users connect where standard Tor traffic or public relay addresses are blocked
attributes.examples_note: Specific transports and availability change over time; use current official Tor documentation.

entities.name: Traffic analysis
entities.description: Inferring communication relationships or activity from traffic patterns such as timing, volume, direction, and connection metadata, even when payload content is encrypted.

entities.name: End-to-end traffic correlation
entities.description: An attack in which an observer compares traffic entering and leaving an anonymity network to infer that flows belong to the same communication.

attributes.limitation: Tor's low-latency design cannot guarantee protection against an adversary able to monitor both ends of a connection.

entities.name: Sybil attack
entities.description: An attack in which one adversary operates or controls multiple identities or nodes to gain disproportionate influence over a distributed system.

entities.name: Malicious or compromised relay
entities.description: A relay controlled by an adversary or compromised in a way that attempts to observe, manipulate, or correlate traffic.

entities.name: Browser fingerprinting
entities.description: Recognition or distinguishing of a browser based on a combination of device and browser attributes such as fonts, screen settings, language, and graphics capabilities.

entities.name: Endpoint compromise
entities.description: Compromise of the user's device, browser, or destination server; network anonymity cannot protect secrets exposed directly at a compromised endpoint.

entities.name: HTTPS / TLS
entities.description: HTTPS protects HTTP traffic between the browser and the TLS endpoint. It remains important when using Tor because Tor does not itself guarantee encryption from the exit relay to a public Internet destination.

entities.name: Exit relay policy
entities.description: Rules governing which destination ports or traffic an exit relay permits; exit operators commonly restrict traffic to reduce abuse and operational risk.

entities.name: Website restrictions on Tor exit traffic
entities.description: A destination service may block, challenge, or limit traffic from known Tor exit IP addresses because many unrelated users share exit relays or because of the site's risk policies.

entities.name: Censorship circumvention
entities.description: Using privacy or networking tools to reach information or communicate when access is blocked or monitored.

entities.name: Whistleblowing and source protection
entities.description: Use of privacy-preserving communication channels to help sources communicate with journalists or organizations while reducing exposure of their identity or location.

entities.name: Online privacy
entities.description: Control over collection, linkage, retention, and disclosure of information about online activities.

entities.name: Anonymity
entities.description: A condition in which an action or communication cannot readily be linked to a specific identity within a defined threat model; anonymity is contextual, not absolute.

entities.name: Clearnet
entities.description: The publicly accessible Internet or, in narrower usage, the indexed surface web; ordinary clearnet browsing commonly exposes a user's public network address to destination services unless mediated.

entities.name: Deep web
entities.description: Web content not indexed by conventional search engines; this includes many ordinary authenticated portals and database-driven resources, not only dark-web services.

entities.name: Dark web
entities.description: Content or services hosted on anonymity-oriented networks such as Tor; it is a subset of content commonly described as deep web, not a synonym for all non-indexed content.

entities.name: United States Naval Research Laboratory
entities.description: Research organization whose researchers developed the core onion-routing concept in the mid-1990s, according to the supplied article.

entities.name: Paul Syverson

entities.name: SecureDrop

entities.name: Censorship and surveillance authorities
entities.description: Governmental or other entities that may block, monitor, or analyze network traffic; the capabilities of any particular observer depend on its position and resources.

history.event: Alpha version of Tor launched as The Onion Routing project
Onion services first specified, according to the supplied article
First public release of Tor, approximately one year after the alpha launch
Naval Research Laboratory released Tor code under a free license; EFF supported continued development
Onion services began deployment on the Tor network, according to the supplied article
The Tor Project was founded as a nonprofit organization
Tor Project disclosed a relay-early traffic-confirmation attack involving malicious relays; affected relays were removed and software was patched, according to the supplied article

public_internet_circuit.component: client application configured to use Tor
public_internet_circuit.action: The application sends supported TCP traffic to a local Tor SOCKS interface or Tor Browser.
The first relay receives traffic from the client; it can see the client's network address but ordinarily not the final destination.
Forwards the circuit to the next hop without being the public Internet exit.
Removes the final Tor relay layer and connects to the public Internet destination; destination typically sees the exit IP.
Receives the request. If the application protocol lacks end-to-end encryption, traffic between exit and destination may be observable or modifiable.

onion_service_connection.action: Knows or obtains the service's .onion address and uses Tor-capable software.
Client obtains service connection information through Tor's distributed directory mechanisms.
Client chooses a path through Tor, including a rendezvous point.
Onion service independently builds a Tor path and connects to the rendezvous point.
Joins the circuits; communication remains within Tor and does not use a public Internet exit.

architecture.important_distinction: Tor routes traffic through relays; it is not a replacement for HTTPS, secure endpoint configuration, or sound operational security.

protected_properties: reduce destination visibility of the client's ordinary public IP
reduce any single relay's ability to see both source and destination
support location privacy and censorship circumvention
support onion services without publishing the host's ordinary IP address
out_of_scope_or_limited_properties: perfect anonymity against global or multi-point traffic observation
protection from malware or a compromised operating system
preventing identification when a user logs into a personal account or reveals identifying details
automatically routing every application on a device through Tor
end-to-end encryption between exit relay and public destination when the application does not provide it
preventing a destination from recognizing or blocking Tor exit IP addresses
attacker_capabilities_to_consider: control or observation of one relay
observation by an ISP or local network
simultaneous observation of traffic entering and leaving Tor
operation of multiple malicious relays (Sybil behavior)
blocking public relays or Tor traffic
mitigations_and_hygiene: Use the official Tor Browser or correctly configured applications.
Keep software updated and obtain it from official project sources.
Use HTTPS for public Internet websites.
Do not assume other applications on the device are routed through Tor.
Avoid logging into identifying accounts when identity separation is the goal.
Do not open downloaded documents in an application that can make unprotected network requests while the user is online unless the risks are understood.
Use bridges or supported pluggable transports where appropriate for censorship circumvention.
Use official Tor Project documentation for current configuration advice.
